Robert Mugabe. Zimbabwe's founding president, leading the nation from Rhodesian white-minority rule to independence in 1980. A nationalist who fought a brutal liberation war, he initially governed with pragmatism and reconciliation but transformed into an authoritarian figure, presiding over economic collapse and repression during his 37-year tenure.

He led the Zimbabwe African National Union, or ZANU, guerrilla movement against Rhodesian white-minority rule during the 1970s Chimurenga War, becoming the dominant liberation figure. He was elected Prime Minister at independence in 1980 and declared reconciliation with white Rhodesians and minorities, earning international credibility and initially governing with relative democratic restraint. Later, he pivoted toward authoritarianism, banning opposition parties, deploying secret police, and purging rivals. While promoting black land reclamation from white farmers—popular domestically—he created economic disruption.

He consolidated presidential power in 1987 when he became President, weakened parliament, and ran increasingly aggressive land seizures from the nineteen-nineties onward, destabilizing agriculture and the economy. He presided over hyperinflation, currency collapse, and widespread poverty in the two-thousands while enriching his family and loyalists, becoming a symbol of postcolonial authoritarianism and corruption. He remained in power until 2017, when the military ousted him. He died in exile in Singapore in 2019. His authoritarian trajectory echoed Idi Amin's brutality and contrasted with the democratic restraint of Nelson Mandela and Julius Nyerere.
